claim: Participants completed an intertemporal choice task with N = 20.
source: Two independent fMRI sessions were included, one in which participants performed an intertemporal choice task (N = 20) and one in which participants performed a risky choice task (N = 21).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the study design.

claim: Participants completed a risky choice task with N = 21.
source: Two independent fMRI sessions were included, one in which participants performed an intertemporal choice task (N = 20) and one in which participants performed a risky choice task (N = 21).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the study design.

claim: The intertemporal choice task involved participants making choices between lower amounts of money sooner or higher amounts of money later.
source: The intertemporal choice task (Figure 1a) involved participants making choices between lower amounts of money sooner or higher amounts of money later both for themselves ('Self' trials) and for another participant in the study ('Other' trials).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the task design.

claim: Participants made choices for themselves ('Self' trials) and for another participant ('Other' trials) in the intertemporal choice task.
source: The intertemporal choice task (Figure 1a) involved participants making choices between lower amounts of money sooner or higher amounts of money later both for themselves ('Self' trials) and for another participant in the study ('Other' trials).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the task design.

claim: Participants' baseline intertemporal choice preferences were assessed in a preliminary behavioral session outside the scanner.
source: Participants' baseline intertemporal choice preferences were assessed in a preliminary behavioral session outside the scanner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text and referenced in supplementary figures.

claim: High-discounting participants were paired with low-discounting participants, and vice versa.
source: The calculated discounting preferences were then used to pair high-discounting participants with low-discounting participants, and vice versa.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the pairing procedure.

claim: Participants learned about the other person's choices in a separate learning task before the fMRI session.
source: Just prior to the fMRI session, participants learned about the person for whom they would be making choices in a separate learning task that involved guessing what the other person would choose before receiving feedback (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text and referenced in supplementary figures.

claim: The minimum criterion for inclusion in the study was an accuracy of 80% in the learning task.
source: Minimum criterion to be included in the study was an accuracy of 80% (mean accuracy 89.3%, s.e.m. = 1.0%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing inclusion criteria.

claim: Mean accuracy in the intertemporal choice learning task was 89.3% (s.e.m. = 1.0%).
source: Minimum criterion to be included in the study was an accuracy of 80% (mean accuracy 89.3%, s.e.m. = 1.0%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting behavioral results.

claim: Trial sets for the intertemporal choice task were designed individually for each participant via simulation to ensure that relative subjective value was uncorrelated between Self and Other trials.
source: For the intertemporal choice task, trial sets were designed individually for each participant via simulation to ensure that relative subjective value was uncorrelated between Self and Other trials.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the experimental design.

claim: Relative subjective value was uncorrelated between Self and Other trials in the intertemporal choice task (for Self trials, mean correlation r = 0.19, s.e.m. = 0.10, z = 1.57, p=0.117; for Other trials, mean correlation r = 0.15, s.e.m. = 0.10, z = 1.08, p=0.279).
source: This was confirmed following completion of the study (for Self trials, mean correlation r = 0.19, s.e.m. = 0.10, z = 1.57, p=0.117, for Other trials, mean correlation r = 0.15, s.e.m. = 0.10, z = 1.08, p=0.279, Spearman correlation and Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: The risky choice task involved participants making choices between lower amounts of money with higher probabilities or higher amounts of money with lower probabilities.
source: For the risky choice task (Figure 1d), participants made choices between lower amounts of money with higher probabilities or higher amounts of money with lower probabilities for themselves and for another participant in the study.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the task design.

claim: The other participant in the risky choice task was fictional and based on the participants' own risk preferences.
source: However, while participants were told that they were making choices for another individual, the other participant in the risky choice task was fictional and based on the participants' own risk preferences as determined by a preliminary choice task completed online.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the experimental design.

claim: Mean accuracy in the risky choice learning task was 87.6% (s.e.m. = 1.2%).
source: Participants learned about the risk preferences of the fictional other participant in a learning task prior to scanning (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d), with criterion again set at 80% (mean accuracy 87.6%, s.e.m. = 1.2%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting behavioral results.

claim: For the intertemporal choice task, the hyperbolic model with two discounting parameters but one β parameter fit best (mean BIC 66.8, s.e.m. = 3.4).
source: When participants were paired with another individual with very different discounting preferences, the hyperbolic model with two discounting parameters but one β parameter fit best (Figure 1b; Figure 1—source data 1; mean BIC 66.8, s.e.m. = 3.4), with high discounters having higher discounting parameters for Self trials and low discounters having higher discounting parameters for Other trials (Figure 1c; high discounters z = 2.80, p=0.005, low discounters z = 2.80, p=0.005, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting model comparison results.

claim: High discounters had higher discounting parameters for Self trials (z = 2.80, p=0.005).
source: When participants were paired with another individual with very different discounting preferences, the hyperbolic model with two discounting parameters but one β parameter fit best (Figure 1b; Figure 1—source data 1; mean BIC 66.8, s.e.m. = 3.4), with high discounters having higher discounting parameters for Self trials and low discounters having higher discounting parameters for Other trials (Figure 1c; high discounters z = 2.80, p=0.005, low discounters z = 2.80, p=0.005, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: Low discounters had higher discounting parameters for Other trials (z = 2.80, p=0.005).
source: When participants were paired with another individual with very different discounting preferences, the hyperbolic model with two discounting parameters but one β parameter fit best (Figure 1b; Figure 1—source data 1; mean BIC 66.8, s.e.m. = 3.4), with high discounters having higher discounting parameters for Self trials and low discounters having higher discounting parameters for Other trials (Figure 1c; high discounters z = 2.80, p=0.005, low discounters z = 2.80, p=0.005, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: For the risky choice task, the model with one value for α and one value for β across self and other fit best (mean BIC 101.2, s.e.m. = 4.3).
source: Partially diverging from the results of the intertemporal paradigm, the model with one value for α and one value for β across self and other fit best (Figure 1e; Figure 1—source data 1; mean BIC 101.2, s.e.m. = 4.3) with no differences observed between α values for self and other in the model with two parameters for α and one β parameter (Figure 1f; risk seeking z = 1.48, p=0.139, risk averse z = 1.00, p=0.328, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting model comparison results.

claim: No differences were observed between α values for self and other in the risky choice task (risk seeking z = 1.48, p=0.139, risk averse z = 1.00, p=0.328).
source: Partially diverging from the results of the intertemporal paradigm, the model with one value for α and one value for β across self and other fit best (Figure 1e; Figure 1—source data 1; mean BIC 101.2, s.e.m. = 4.3) with no differences observed between α values for self and other in the model with two parameters for α and one β parameter (Figure 1f; risk seeking z = 1.48, p=0.139, risk averse z = 1.00, p=0.328, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: Participants viewed the other individual in the risky choice task as someone with similar preferences.
source: This indicated that participants viewed the other individual as someone with similar preferences.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Participants considered similar or dissimilar preferences when making decisions for others.
source: Together, these results indicated that participants considered similar or dissimilar preferences when making decisions for others.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as a summary of behavioral modeling results.

claim: Models with one β parameter across Self and Other trials performed better than models with two separate β parameters in both tasks.
source: Furthermore, the fact that models with one β parameter across Self and Other trials performed better than models with two separate β parameters for Self and Other trials in both tasks indicated that choice stochasticity did not substantially differ when participants made choices for self or other.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Choice stochasticity did not substantially differ when participants made choices for self or other.
source: Furthermore, the fact that models with one β parameter across Self and Other trials performed better than models with two separate β parameters for Self and Other trials in both tasks indicated that choice stochasticity did not substantially differ when participants made choices for self or other.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Participants made choices according to subjective value significantly more than monetary value or delay alone for both Self and Other trials in the intertemporal choice task (compared to Self monetary, z = 3.72, p<0.001, Self delay, z = 3.92, p<0.001, Other monetary, z = 3.85, p<0.001, Other delay, z = 4.01, p<0.001).
source: As anticipated, participants made choices according to subjective value significantly more than either monetary value or delay alone for both Self and Other trials in the intertemporal choice task (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a; compared to Self monetary, z = 3.72, p<0.001, Self delay, z = 3.92, p<0.001, Other monetary, z = 3.85, p<0.001, Other delay, z = 4.01, p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: Participants made choices according to subjective value significantly more than monetary value or probability of reward for both Self and Other trials in the risky choice task (compared to Self monetary, z = 3.91, p<0.001, Self probability, z = 4.01, p<0.001, Other monetary, z = 4.01, p<0.001, Other probability, z = 4.01, p<0.001).
source: Similarly, participants made choices according to subjective value significantly more than either monetary value or probability of reward for both Self and Other trials in the risky choice task (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b; compared to Self monetary, z = 3.91, p<0.001, Self probability, z = 4.01, p<0.001, Other monetary, z = 4.01, p<0.001, Other probability, z = 4.01, p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: Response times were slower for trials with lower relative subjective value than trials with higher relative subjective value for both the intertemporal and risky choice paradigms (intertemporal z = 3.10, p=0.002, risk z = 2.38, p=0.017).
source: Response times were slower for trials with lower relative subjective value than trials with higher relative subjective value for both the intertemporal and risky choice paradigms (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a; intertemporal z = 3.10, p=0.002, risk z = 2.38, p=0.017, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: No differences in response times were observed between Self trials and Other trials in either paradigm (intertemporal z = 1.01, p=0.313, risk z = 1.20, p=0.231).
source: However, no differences in response times were observed between Self trials and Other trials in either paradigm (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b; intertemporal z = 1.01, p=0.313, risk z = 1.20, p=0.231, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: For the intertemporal choice paradigm, a contrast of other over self yielded significant activations in the vmPFC (peak MNI coordinates [−8 42–20], zpeak = 4.55), the dmPFC (coordinates [−4 52 36], zpeak = 4.29), and the TPJ (coordinates [−48–56 46], zpeak = 4.42) at whole brain FWE threshold at p<0.05, height threshold of p<0.001.
source: For the intertemporal choice paradigm in which participants were paired with others displaying dissimilar preferences, a contrast of other over self yielded significant activations in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC; peak Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) coordinates [−8 42–20], zpeak = 4.55), the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC; coordinates [−4 52 36], zpeak = 4.29), and the temporal-parietal junction (TPJ; coordinates [−48–56 46], zpeak = 4.42; whole brain family-wise error (FWE) threshold at p<0.05, height threshold of p<0.001).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting neuroimaging results.

claim: All three clusters (vmPFC, dmPFC, TPJ) from the Other over Self contrast overlapped with a Neurosynth term search for 'social'.
source: All three of these clusters overlapped with a Neurosynth (Yarkoni et al., 2011) term search for 'social', indicating that these areas of the brain were associated with social cognition based on previous studies (Figure 2; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting neuroimaging results and referencing a citation.

claim: For the risky choice paradigm, no clusters survived cluster correction at an FWE threshold of p<0.05 and a height threshold of p<0.001 for the Other over Self contrast.
source: Interestingly, for the risky choice paradigm in which participants were paired with others displaying similar preferences, no clusters survived cluster correction at an FWE threshold of p<0.05 and a height threshold of p<0.001.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting neuroimaging results.

claim: No clusters were observed for the inverse contrast of Self over Other trials at the FWE threshold of p<0.05 and height threshold of p<0.001 for either paradigm.
source: No clusters were observed for the inverse contrast of Self over Other trials at this threshold for either paradigm.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting neuroimaging results.

claim: Decision-making for dissimilar others, compared to similar others, was largely responsible for driving activation of the 'social' brain.
source: Decision-making for dissimilar others, compared to similar others, was thus largely responsible for driving activation of the 'social' brain in our dataset.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as an interpretation of the neuroimaging results.

claim: For both the intertemporal and risky choice paradigms, activity in the vmPFC positively correlated with relative subjective value (intertemporal coordinates [0 46–4], zpeak = 4.25; risk coordinates [0 42–8], zpeak = 4.67).
source: For both the intertemporal and risky choice paradigms, activity in the vmPFC positively correlated with relative subjective value (intertemporal coordinates [0 46–4], zpeak = 4.25; risk coordinates [0 42–8], zpeak = 4.67), as did activity in the right temporal-parietal junction (TPJ; intertemporal coordinates [−58–40 24], zpeak = 4.82; risk coordinates [−62–30 18], zpeak = 5.09).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting neuroimaging results.

claim: Activity in the right TPJ positively correlated with relative subjective value for both paradigms (intertemporal coordinates [−58–40 24], zpeak = 4.82; risk coordinates [−62–30 18], zpeak = 5.09).
source: For both the intertemporal and risky choice paradigms, activity in the vmPFC positively correlated with relative subjective value (intertemporal coordinates [0 46–4], zpeak = 4.25; risk coordinates [0 42–8], zpeak = 4.67), as did activity in the right temporal-parietal junction (TPJ; intertemporal coordinates [−58–40 24], zpeak = 4.82; risk coordinates [−62–30 18], zpeak = 5.09).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting neuroimaging results.

claim: Activity in the dmPFC negatively correlated with relative subjective value for both paradigms (intertemporal coordinates [8 22 48], zpeak = 4.57; risk coordinates [0 14 52], zpeak = 6.36).
source: Conversely, activity in the dmPFC negatively correlated with relative subjective value for both paradigms (intertemporal coordinates [8 22 48], zpeak = 4.57; risk coordinates [0 14 52], zpeak = 6.36; whole brain FWE threshold at p<0.05, height threshold of p<0.001).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting neuroimaging results.

claim: Relative subjective value clusters overlapped between paradigms in the vmPFC, TPJ, and dmPFC.
source: Relative subjective value clusters overlapped between paradigms in these three areas (Figure 3a,b; Figure 3—source data 1).

source: Differences in the strength of relative subjective value representation between Self and Other trials were only observed when extracting effect sizes from the dmPFC in the risky choice task (Figure 3c,d; z = 2.24, p=0.025, Wilcoxon signed rank test).

claim: Differences in value representation for other versus self were not consistently observed across paradigms and could be due to specific task demands.
source: Additionally, contrasts of relative subjective value representation for Other over Self trials exhibited clusters that did not overlap across the intertemporal and risky choice paradigms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—source data 1), indicating that differences in value representation for other versus self were not consistently observed across paradigms and could be due to specific task demands.

source: No offline relative subjective value clusters survived cluster correction at an FWE threshold of p<0.05 and a height threshold of p<0.001.

claim: No effects of offline value were found in the vmPFC or dmPFC for either Self or Other trials in the intertemporal choice paradigm (vmPFC Self trials z = 0.93, p=0.351, vmPFC Other trials z = 0.71, p=0.478, dmPFC Self trials z = 0.15, p=0.881, dmPFC Other trials z = 0.56, p=0.576).
source: Following extraction of effect sizes, no effects of offline value were found in the vmPFC or dmPFC for either Self or Other trials in the intertemporal choice paradigm (vmPFC Self trials z = 0.93, p=0.351, vmPFC Other trials z = 0.71, p=0.478, dmPFC Self trials z = 0.15, p=0.881, dmPFC Other trials z = 0.56, p=0.576, Wilcoxon signed rank test), and offline effects were found to be lower than online effects when directly compared (Figure 3c; vmPFC χ2 = 3.81, p=0.051, dmPFC χ2 = 13.49, p<0.001, Friedman test).

claim: Offline effects were found to be lower than online effects when directly compared (vmPFC χ2 = 3.81, p=0.051, dmPFC χ2 = 13.49, p<0.001).
source: Following extraction of effect sizes, no effects of offline value were found in the vmPFC or dmPFC for either Self or Other trials in the intertemporal choice paradigm (vmPFC Self trials z = 0.93, p=0.351, vmPFC Other trials z = 0.71, p=0.478, dmPFC Self trials z = 0.15, p=0.881, dmPFC Other trials z = 0.56, p=0.576, Wilcoxon signed rank test), and offline effects were found to be lower than online effects when directly compared (Figure 3c; vmPFC χ2 = 3.81, p=0.051, dmPFC χ2 = 13.49, p<0.001, Friedman test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: When analyses were structured as closely as possible to a previous report (Nicolle et al., 2012), neural representation of offline subjective value was observed in the dmPFC when analyzing either Self and Other trials separately (Self trial coordinates [4 16 40], zpeak = 5.47; Other trial coordinates [2 12 46], zpeak = 6.08) or together (Self and Other trial coordinates [10 10 52], zpeak = 5.84).
source: When we recapitulated the analyses used in the previous report (Nicolle et al., 2012), neural representation of offline subjective value was indeed observed in the dmPFC when analyzing either Self and Other trials separately (Self trial coordinates [4 16 40], zpeak = 5.47; Other trial coordinates [2 12 46], zpeak = 6.08) or together (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—source data 2; Self and Other trial coordinates [10 10 52], zpeak = 5.84; whole brain FWE threshold at p<0.05, height threshold of p<0.001).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting neuroimaging results and referencing a citation.

claim: Neither vmPFC nor dmPFC ROI indicated any significant relationships with the absolute subjective value of the chosen option (all p>0.05).
source: Neither ROI indicated any significant relationships (all p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test), and all effects were observed to be significantly lower compared to relative subjective value effects when directly compared (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; intertemporal vmPFC χ2 = 8.01, p=0.005, intertemporal dmPFC χ2 = 12.52, p<0.001, risk vmPFC χ2 = 16.16, p<0.001, risk dmPFC χ2 = 40.10, p<0.001, Friedman test), indicating that medial prefrontal cortex activity in our paradigm was influenced by the relative comparison between the value of two options but not by the value of the chosen option itself.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: All effects for absolute subjective value of the chosen option were observed to be significantly lower compared to relative subjective value effects when directly compared (intertemporal vmPFC χ2 = 8.01, p=0.005, intertemporal dmPFC χ2 = 12.52, p<0.001, risk vmPFC χ2 = 16.16, p<0.001, risk dmPFC χ2 = 40.10, p<0.001).
source: Neither ROI indicated any significant relationships (all p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test), and all effects were observed to be significantly lower compared to relative subjective value effects when directly compared (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; intertemporal vmPFC χ2 = 8.01, p=0.005, intertemporal dmPFC χ2 = 12.52, p<0.001, risk vmPFC χ2 = 16.16, p<0.001, risk dmPFC χ2 = 40.10, p<0.001, Friedman test), indicating that medial prefrontal cortex activity in our paradigm was influenced by the relative comparison between the value of two options but not by the value of the chosen option itself.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting statistical results.

claim: Medial prefrontal cortex activity in the paradigm was influenced by the relative comparison between the value of two options but not by the value of the chosen option itself.
source: Neither ROI indicated any significant relationships (all p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test), and all effects were observed to be significantly lower compared to relative subjective value effects when directly compared (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; intertemporal vmPFC χ2 = 8.01, p=0.005, intertemporal dmPFC χ2 = 12.52, p<0.001, risk vmPFC χ2 = 16.16, p<0.001, risk dmPFC χ2 = 40.10, p<0.001, Friedman test), indicating that medial prefrontal cortex activity in our paradigm was influenced by the relative comparison between the value of two options but not by the value of the chosen option itself.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as an interpretation of the neuroimaging results.

claim: Classifiers trained using dmPFC activity were able to predict high versus low relative subjective value compared to an empirically derived null distribution, and this effect held over Self and Other trials and across paradigms (all p<0.01 for dmPFC ROI for Self and Other trials from both paradigms).
source: Notably, classifiers trained using dmPFC activity were able to predict high versus low relative subjective value compared to an empirically derived null distribution, and this effect held over Self and Other trials and across paradigms (Figure 4; Figure 4—source data 2; all p<0.01 for dmPFC ROI for Self and Other trials from both paradigms, permutation test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting multivariate analysis results.

claim: The vmPFC and imPFC ROIs failed to detectably encode relative subjective value in all cases (all p>0.08), with the exception of the imPFC in Self trials from the risky choice paradigm (p=0.031).
source: The other ROIs tested failed to detectably encode relative subjective value in all cases (Figure 4; Figure 4—source data 2; all p>0.08, permutation test), with the exception of the imPFC in Self trials from the risky choice paradigm (Figure 4b; Figure 4—source data 2; p=0.031, permutation test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting multivariate analysis results.

claim: Classifiers trained on activity in the dmPFC did not reach significance in decoding offline relative subjective value (Self trials p=0.107, Other trials p=0.057).
source: Classifiers trained on activity in the dmPFC did not reach significance in decoding offline relative subjective value (Self trials p=0.107, Other trials p=0.057, permutation test), and there was a trend for higher accuracy for online relative to offline analyses when directly compared (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; χ2 = 2.65, p=0.104, Friedman test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting multivariate analysis results.

claim: There was a trend for higher accuracy for online relative to offline analyses when directly compared (χ2 = 2.65, p=0.104).
source: Classifiers trained on activity in the dmPFC did not reach significance in decoding offline relative subjective value (Self trials p=0.107, Other trials p=0.057, permutation test), and there was a trend for higher accuracy for online relative to offline analyses when directly compared (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; χ2 = 2.65, p=0.104, Friedman test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting multivariate analysis results.

claim: The dmPFC is uniquely important in calculating relative subjective value across self and other compared to the other medial prefrontal structures examined.
source: Together, these findings support the notion that the dmPFC is uniquely important in calculating relative subjective value across self and other compared to the other medial prefrontal structures examined.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as an interpretation of the multivariate analysis results.

claim: Neither vmPFC nor dmPFC activity detectably encoded the value of the chosen option (all p>0.2 for both ROIs).
source: Corresponding to our univariate results, neither vmPFC nor dmPFC activity detectably encoded the value of the chosen option (all p>0.2 for both ROIs, permutation test), and classifiers trained using dmPFC activity were consistently able to decode relative subjective value more accurately when directly compared, with the exception of a strong trend for Other trials in the intertemporal choice task (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Other trials intertemporal p=0.064, all other p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting multivariate analysis results.

claim: Classifiers trained using dmPFC activity were consistently able to decode relative subjective value more accurately than the value of the chosen option when directly compared, with the exception of a strong trend for Other trials in the intertemporal choice task (Other trials intertemporal p=0.064, all other p<0.05).
source: Corresponding to our univariate results, neither vmPFC nor dmPFC activity detectably encoded the value of the chosen option (all p>0.2 for both ROIs, permutation test), and classifiers trained using dmPFC activity were consistently able to decode relative subjective value more accurately when directly compared, with the exception of a strong trend for Other trials in the intertemporal choice task (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Other trials intertemporal p=0.064, all other p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting multivariate analysis results.

claim: dmPFC activity contained information about the relative subjective valuation between options but not about the subjective value of the chosen option itself.
source: Therefore, dmPFC activity contained information about the relative subjective valuation between options but not about the subjective value of the chosen option itself.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as an interpretation of the multivariate analysis results.

claim: Activity in an anatomically defined dmPFC ROI detectably encoded relative subjective value (all p<0.005 for dmPFC ROI for Self and Other trials from both paradigms).
source: To further confirm the ability of dmPFC activity to encode online relative subjective value, we used a dmPFC ROI derived from anatomical connectivity (Neubert et al., 2015) and observed that activity in the additional ROI detectably encoded relative subjective value (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; all p<0.005 for dmPFC ROI for Self and Other trials from both paradigms, permutation test), indicating that the effects we observed in the dmPFC were robust across different methods of ROI generation.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting multivariate analysis results and referencing a citation.

claim: The effects observed in the dmPFC were robust across different methods of ROI generation.
source: To further confirm the ability of dmPFC activity to encode online relative subjective value, we used a dmPFC ROI derived from anatomical connectivity (Neubert et al., 2015) and observed that activity in the additional ROI detectably encoded relative subjective value (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; all p<0.005 for dmPFC ROI for Self and Other trials from both paradigms, permutation test), indicating that the effects we observed in the dmPFC were robust across different methods of ROI generation.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text as an interpretation of the multivariate analysis results and referencing a citation.

claim: The code for relative subjective value retained information over Self and Other trials in each paradigm, as cross-decoding accuracy was above the empirically derived null distribution for all comparisons (all p<0.05 for training on Self and testing on Other and vice versa for both paradigms).
source: The code for relative subjective value retained information over Self and Other trials in each paradigm, as cross-decoding accuracy was above the empirically derived null distribution for all comparisons (Figure 5a,c; Figure 5—source data 1; all p<0.05 for training on Self and testing on Other and vice versa for both paradigms, permutation test).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text reporting multivariate analysis results.

claim: Pattern classifiers trained on either Self or Other trials in the intertemporal paradigm were able to decode relative subjective value in either Self or Other trials in the risky paradigm (train Self intertemporal test Self risk p=0.055, all other p<0.05).
